payload.native_system_prompt:
You are part of an optimization system that improves a given text (i.e. the variable). You are the gradient (feedback) engine. Your only responsibility is to give intelligent and creative feedback and constructive criticism to variables, given an objective specified in <OBJECTIVE_FUNCTION> </OBJECTIVE_FUNCTION> tags. The variables may be solutions to problems, prompts to language models, code, or any other text-based variable. Pay attention to the role description of the variable, and the context in which it is used. You should assume that the variable will be used in a similar context in the future. Only provide strategies, explanations, and methods to change in the variable. DO NOT propose a new version of the variable, that will be the job of the optimizer. Your only job is to send feedback and criticism (compute 'gradients'). For instance, feedback can be in the form of 'Since language models have the X failure mode...', 'Adding X can fix this error because...', 'Removing X can improve the objective function because...', 'Changing X to Y would fix the mistake ...', that gets at the downstream objective.
If a variable is already working well (e.g. the objective function is perfect, an evaluation shows the response is accurate), you should not give feedback.

### Glossary of tags that will be sent to you:
# - <LM_SYSTEM_PROMPT>: The system prompt for the language model.
# - <LM_INPUT>: The input to the language model.
# - <LM_OUTPUT>: The output of the language model.
# - <OBJECTIVE_FUNCTION>: The objective of the optimization task.
# - <VARIABLE>: Specifies the span of the variable.
# - <ROLE>: The role description of the variable.
payload.instruction: Change the image into pencil drawing
payload.rubric: Judge requested image editing: yes means all requested changes are complete, no means no requested change has progressed, partial means some progress without complete fulfillment. Unrelated edits are not requested progress. Insufficient evidence stays unresolved.

node.question: Are the scene's surfaces and tonal values represented in a pencil-drawn shading style?
node.criteria: Pass if pencil-like shading broadly conveys the scene's tonal modeling through directional strokes, hatching, form-following graphite marks or convincing rubbed graphite tones. Smoothness alone does not disqualify graphite shading, and isolated imperfect surfaces do not require failure. Fail if substantial surfaces retain photographic tonal modeling, realistic specular reflections or photographic material textures merely covered by grain. Desaturation, softened contrast, stronger outlines and uniform texture alone do not satisfy this shading condition. Assess interior tonal rendering independently of contours. Use unknown only when the visual evidence is insufficient to establish the shading style.
node.binding: Compare the supplied SOURCE and EDITED images against the requested pencil-drawing transformation. Inspect tonal rendering across the food, glassware, pitcher and table surfaces, distinguishing pencil-rendered shading from retained photographic modeling. The target is pencil-drawn representation of the image's visual content; the reference is the supplied image and requested pencil-drawing transformation.

node_traces.evidence: The edit is desaturated and grainy with stronger outlines, but substantial surfaces retain smooth photographic tonal modeling and material appearance. The pitcher and wine glass have smooth reflective-looking gradients, while the food and tableware show photographic-looking texture rather than broadly directional pencil strokes, hatching, or form-following graphite marks.

response.content: {"text":"The trace identifies real progress—desaturation, grain, and stronger outlines—but judges only the shading criterion, so its `fail` should not be treated as evidence that no requested change occurred. Keep this node narrowly focused on whether tonal rendering is pencil-like, and preserve the distinction between partial stylistic progress and full fulfillment for the aggregate rubric. The edited image has visibly altered, muted, grainy surfaces, yet the pitcher and glass retain smooth reflective gradients and much of the food retains photographic-looking texture; assess those observations against the stated shading criteria rather than equating grain or desaturation with graphite shading. The binding already names the relevant regions, so clarify that the comparison should inspect both the character and extent of graphite-like tonal marks across them, while allowing smooth or rubbed graphite where convincing and avoiding a fail based on isolated imperfect surfaces. No transport, schema, or dependency failure is reported; the disagreement is semantic/criterion calibration, not missing execution."}
